Radio station email list for music promotion: buyer's guide

By the RadioReach team Updated August 19, 2026 2 min read Templates & press kits

On this page
  • The fields a contact list should contain
  • A seven-point quality test
  • Turn a list into a qualified campaign
  • Permission, privacy, and deliverability
  • Questions to ask before buying

A useful radio station email list shortens contact research. A bad one creates bounces, complaints, wasted hours, and a damaged sender reputation. The difference is not the largest number printed on the sales page; it is whether the records identify relevant professional roles, show enough context to qualify a station, and can be checked against current first-party sources.

The fields a contact list should contain

FieldWhy it matters
Station and locationLets you verify identity, market, and local relevance.
RoleSeparates music directors and programmers from irrelevant departments.
Email or submission routeProvides a starting point—not proof of perpetual validity.
Station type and formatSupports initial filtering before playlist-level research.
Source / checked dateMakes freshness auditable and prioritizes re-verification.

A seven-point quality test

  1. Role clarity: named music roles beat unlabeled addresses.
  2. First-party provenance: official station sources are stronger than unexplained aggregation.
  3. Freshness: the seller acknowledges staff turnover and states when data was compiled or checked.
  4. Coverage honesty: “contact” does not silently mean every record has a personal email.
  5. Useful segmentation: location and role are present; genre still needs playlist verification.
  6. No airplay promise: contacts do not buy editorial outcomes.
  7. Clear terms: usage restrictions, refund terms, and privacy obligations are visible before purchase.

Turn a list into a qualified campaign

  1. Filter by territory, station type, and likely format.
  2. Visit each priority station's official site and current schedule.
  3. Confirm the role, submission policy, and recent playlist fit.
  4. Add a source URL and checked date to your working sheet.
  5. Send individually, in small waves, with one relevant follow-up.
  6. Suppress opt-outs and hard bounces immediately.

This verification layer matters because radio staffing and programming change constantly. Even a recently checked address can change tomorrow.

Permission, privacy, and deliverability

Purchasing access to business contact research does not create blanket consent. Applicable rules vary by recipient and country, including CAN-SPAM, CASL, UK privacy and electronic-marketing rules, Australia's Spam Act, and other laws. Use transparent sender information, truthful subjects, relevant one-to-one messages, and a working way to opt out. Never harvest addresses, rotate domains to evade filters, or continue after an objection.

Questions to ask before buying

  • Exactly which fields are included in every record?
  • How are addresses sourced and what does “verified” mean?
  • When was the resource last compiled or checked?
  • Are generic and named addresses counted separately?
  • Which countries and station types are covered?
  • What usage is prohibited by the license?
  • Is the format actually usable for the workflow you plan?

Frequently asked questions

What should a legitimate radio station email list include?

At minimum: station name, location, contact role, address, source or provenance, and a meaningful verification or update date. Genre, station type, and submission-policy fields make targeting much safer.

Can I email every address at once?

No. A contact list is a research aid, not permission to blast. Verify priority contacts, select only relevant stations, personalize each message, and comply with the laws and station policies that apply.

Does an email list guarantee radio airplay?

No. No legitimate contact resource can guarantee editorial decisions. It can reduce research time; the station still decides whether the release fits.
